{"schema":"voice-draft-source/4","kind":"draft","draft":"If a manufacturer can reach into a device after sale and switch off a feature, you don't fully own that device. You may possess the plastic, keep it on your desk, and bear every cost when it breaks, but the maker still holds a hidden lever. Ownership has been split: you get custody and liability; the company keeps command. That isn't a sale in the ordinary sense. It's a tenancy dressed up with a receipt.

The practical test is simple. After the money changes hands, who gets the final say over lawful uses of the machine? If you can replace the battery, install software, or keep a paid-for capability only until somebody elsewhere changes a database entry, your control is conditional. The remote switch may be described as “service management” (a phrase that makes confiscation sound like housekeeping), but the mechanism is plain: the seller can revise the bargain after the buyer has performed every part of it.

Of course, a maker sometimes needs to patch dangerous code, revoke stolen credentials, or shut down a service that costs money to operate. None of that requires pretending the buyer owns what the maker still governs. Security updates can preserve capabilities; service contracts can state their terms; network functions can carry clear expiration dates (before the purchase, in language a normal person can understand). The distinction I care about isn't whether software changes. It's whether the change serves your control or overrides it.

Manufacturers will say they must retain discretion because connected products are complicated. Complicated for whom? The complexity lives in a system the seller designed, and it shouldn't become a deed restriction smuggled into your property. When “smart” means “obedient to its former owner,” the intelligence is mostly bullshit. You bought a machine – not a vote in the manufacturer's continuing product strategy. I wouldn't accept that arrangement for a chair or a drill, and adding a radio shouldn't make the trick respectable.

This power changes markets too. A device that can be degraded from afar carries a threat into resale, repair, competition, and daily use. The buyer can't confidently transfer what the seller can later withdraw (even if the hardware remains perfectly capable). Independent repair becomes a game played on the manufacturer's board, with the manufacturer writing new rules mid-turn – the pieces are yours, but the referee works for someone else. We can see the core move without naming a particular product: preserve the asset, revoke the permission, blame the owner's expectations.

I use the word “permission” deliberately. If continued operation depends on the maker's grace, the purchase has acquired a license-shaped trap (without necessarily calling itself a license). A license can be a legitimate bargain when its limits are explicit. A supposed sale that secretly behaves like one is a bait-and-switch – ownership at checkout, permission thereafter. You shouldn't have to study network logs or corporate mood swings to discover which part of your property can vanish.

Law and product design should follow the same rule: after a sale, remote authority over a device must default to its owner. A maker that wants an exception can ask for informed consent, define the narrow purpose, and make the dependency visible at purchase (including what happens when servers or subscriptions end). It can't reserve an all-purpose kill switch merely because code makes one convenient. I don't object to a service ending; I object to the seller reaching through the service to amputate the thing already sold.

We should name the parties correctly. The person who paid is the owner; the company with a revocation key is a continuing governor. We can permit that power in tightly stated cases, but we shouldn't let it hide inside “features,” accounts, or terms that can change later. Otherwise every device becomes the same rigged game: your money buys the pieces, while someone across the network keeps a hand on the board. We aren't choosing between ownership and innovation. We're choosing whether ownership will mean control – and whether the devices we depend on will answer to us.","omitted":[],"refused":""}
